strengths: Addresses a real and underexplored limitation of MoE models: once an expert is selected it is always executed at full capacity, creating discontinuous accuracy-compute trade-offs.

The proposed slimmable-expert design is architecturally simple, requires no change to the standard MoE training pipeline, and the two-width sampling training recipe (full width + one random width per step) is a practical, low-overhead way to instill multi-width capability.

Extensive experimental sweep across model sizes (55M-1B), routing configurations (E8A2/E8A4/E16A4), and token budgets (3B-15B), consistently showing MoSE (TTT) shifts the Pareto frontier relative to uniform-width execution and vanilla MoE.

The lightweight test-time training (TTT) mechanism for learning a router-probability-to-width mapping (single scalar or per-layer γ) is an elegant, cheap adaptation strategy, and the ablation (uniform vs normalized-probability vs TTT) clearly isolates its contribution.
Additional analyses (γ interpretability, FLOPs breakdown, width-wise training dynamics, routing transfer, γ transferability across datasets) add useful diagnostic depth.
weaknesses: All experiments are on very small-scale GPT-2 style models (55M-1B parameters) trained on relatively tiny token budgets (3B-15B tokens), far below the scale of modern production MoE LLMs; it is unclear whether the slimming/TTT approach and its gains hold at scale, with larger vocabularies, longer training, or more experts.

No empirical comparison to the elastic-MoE baselines discussed in Related Work (RoE, EMoE), despite these being the most directly relevant competing methods; the paper only compares against a static vanilla MoE baseline, limiting the ability to judge relative significance.

Efficiency claims are based solely on theoretical FLOPs per token; there is no wall-clock latency/throughput measurement, and slicing variable-width matrix multiplications may not translate into actual hardware speedups (e.g., due to irregular shapes, kernel/memory-bandwidth bottlenecks, or batched execution with heterogeneous widths across tokens/experts in real serving systems).

The core slimming mechanism (nested/ordered channel slicing) is a direct, largely unmodified application of pre-existing slimmable-network techniques (Yu et al. 2019, Tastan et al. 2025a) to MoE FFNs; the main novelty is combinatorial/integrative rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and this positioning could be made more explicit.

Results appear to be single-run (no seeds/variance reported), which is a concern given the paper's own acknowledgment that accuracy metrics exhibit noise and non-monotonic fluctuations (Figure 9 discussion).

Training cost is effectively doubled (two forward/backward passes per step) to obtain the slimmable model, but this additional training overhead is not weighed against the inference-time savings in an overall compute accounting, potentially overstating net efficiency gains.

The calibration set for test-time training is drawn from the same corpus (OpenWebText) used for the main pretraining/eval numbers in Table 1, raising a minor concern about whether reported gains partly reflect calibration-domain overlap rather than a purely general-purpose mechanism (partially addressed by the LAMBADA transfer experiment, but only for perplexity, not the main results table).

Discussion of limitations is fairly thin, mainly noting small model scale and post-training applicability as open questions; there is no discussion of how slimmable experts interact with expert-parallel distributed serving infrastructure, which is central to practical MoE deployment.

strengths: The core idea of decoupling expert selection (which experts) from expert capacity (how much of each expert) is a reasonable and underexplored extension of MoE conditional computation, combining ideas from slimmable networks with MoE routing.

The training recipe (two-width stochastic sampling per iteration) is simple to implement and the paper shows training stability is preserved relative to a vanilla MoE baseline (Figure 3, Appendix B.3).

The experimental sweep is reasonably broad in terms of varying model scale (55M-1B), routing configuration (E8A2/E8A4/E16A4), and token budget (3B-15B), with consistent-looking Pareto frontier improvements from the test-time training (TTT) width-identification mechanism.

The paper includes several useful diagnostic analyses, such as the FLOPs breakdown (Appendix B.2), the learned gamma heatmaps (Appendix B.1), and ablations isolating uniform-width vs. normalized-probability vs. TTT inference modes (Figure 10).
weaknesses: No empirical comparison against the most directly relevant competing methods discussed in Related Work (RoE and Elastic MoE/EMoE), despite the paper explicitly claiming to 'bridge these lines of work.' Without such comparisons, the significance of the proposed approach relative to existing elastic-MoE alternatives cannot be assessed.

All efficiency claims rely solely on theoretical MFLOPs/token; no wall-clock latency, throughput, or hardware-realized speedup is reported. Per-token variable-width execution implies ragged/irregular computation across a batch, which is known to be difficult to realize as actual speedup on GPUs/accelerators; this critical practical concern is never addressed.

Experiments are restricted to very small GPT-2-style models (55M-1B parameters) trained on only 3-15B tokens of a single corpus (OpenWebText), which is far from the scale of modern MoE LLMs (e.g., Mixtral, DeepSeek-MoE) the paper repeatedly references in the introduction. It is unclear whether the training recipe, TTT calibration, and width-sensitivity results transfer to larger, more modern architectures (SwiGLU, RMSNorm, larger expert counts).

The evaluation suite is narrow (perplexity on 2 corpora, LAMBADA, and a 273-example WSC split); no broader reasoning/knowledge benchmarks (e.g., MMLU-style tasks) are used, and results on WSC are noisy and occasionally non-monotonic/inconsistent across configurations (e.g., Table 1 GPT2-Standard/3B shows MoE WSC accuracy exceeding MoSE TTT), undermining the 'consistent' improvement narrative.

No error bars, variance estimates, or multiple seeds are reported anywhere, making it difficult to judge whether the reported gains (often a few tenths of a perplexity point or a percent or two of accuracy) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The 'test-time training' contribution reduces to fitting a single scalar or small per-layer scalar set (gamma) via 50 calibration batches—an extremely simple one-parameter calibration rather than a substantive new learning procedure; its characterization as a methodological contribution is somewhat oversold relative to its complexity.

Missing an important baseline: training/comparing several separately-sized (fixed-width) MoE models at each compute budget point, to verify whether a single elastic MoSE model actually matches dedicated models of matching cost, rather than only comparing against full-width MoE and a within-model uniform-width ablation.

The interaction between variable expert width and MoE capacity/load-balancing mechanisms (token dropping, capacity factor) is not discussed or analyzed, despite being a plausible confound when combining slimming with sparse routing capacity constraints.

The claimed 'simple and stable' training recipe is not compared against alternative sampling strategies (e.g., more than two widths, or different width distributions), so it is unclear whether the specific two-width choice is optimal or merely convenient.

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap in MoE literature: computation is coarse-grained because experts are either fully active or inactive. Decoupling expert selection (which) from expert capacity (how much) is a sensible and reasonably novel architectural idea.

The slimmable-expert mechanism is simple to implement (nested weight slicing), requires no changes to the standard MoE training pipeline besides the dual-width loss, and the paper shows stable training dynamics that closely track vanilla MoE (Fig. 3, Fig. 13).

Broad empirical sweep: three model scales (55M-1B), multiple routing configurations (E8A2/E8A4/E16A4), and multiple token budgets (3B-15B), with consistent qualitative trends throughout, which strengthens confidence that the effect is not a one-off artifact.

The proposed test-time training (TTT) procedure for the sharpness parameter γ is lightweight (one or a handful of scalars, 50 calibration batches), keeps all pretrained weights frozen, and gives a principled, data-driven alternative to fixed heuristics for width allocation.

Useful auxiliary analyses: ablation separating uniform-width vs. normalized-probability vs. TTT (Fig. 10), inference-time routing transfer with a fixed checkpoint (Fig. 8), cross-dataset γ transferability (Fig. 9), and a FLOPs breakdown motivating why targeting expert width is effective (Fig. 12).
Reasonably thorough reproducibility details in the appendix (hyperparameters, optimizer settings, architecture/routing configurations, compute reporting methodology).
weaknesses: Potentially unfair training-compute accounting: MoSE's pretraining objective runs the model twice per step (full width + a random width) and backpropagates through both, which roughly doubles the per-iteration training FLOPs relative to the vanilla MoE baseline. The paper never reports or discusses this training-time compute overhead, only inference-time FLOPs, so the headline claim that MoSE "matches or improves" MoE while being more efficient is only established for inference, not training, and this should be stated explicitly as a caveat/limitation.

No comparison to the other elastic-MoE baselines discussed in Related Work (RoE, EMoE) or to simpler alternatives (e.g., distillation of small dense experts, structured pruning, or standard width-adaptive FFN approaches like MatFormer/slimmable networks applied naively to MoE). The only baseline is vanilla full-width MoE, which somewhat limits how the significance of the contribution can be judged relative to prior elastic-compute methods.

All experiments are at small scale (55M-1B parameters, 3-15B training tokens, GPT-2-style decoder LMs on OpenWebText). It remains unclear whether the training recipe, the magnitude of gains, and the learned γ behavior generalize to billion-to-trillion-parameter MoE LLMs used in practice, where routing dynamics and expert specialization differ substantially.

Reported gains are often numerically small (e.g., OpenWebText PPL 31.03 → 30.81 for GPT2-Small at 15B tokens; 20.81 → 20.38 for GPT2-Standard) and no variance/seeds are reported, so it is hard to assess whether improvements are statistically meaningful versus noise, especially for the low-sample WSC benchmark (273 examples) and LAMBADA accuracy, which the paper itself acknowledges is noisy.

All efficiency claims rely solely on theoretical FLOPs counts; no wall-clock latency or throughput measurements are provided. Dynamic width slicing (variable matrix dimensions per token/expert) can introduce kernel-launch, memory-access, and batching irregularities on real hardware that are not captured by FLOPs, so the practical speedup is unverified.

The paper only demonstrates training MoSE from scratch; the discussion itself flags that post-hoc conversion of existing pretrained MoE checkpoints into slimmable experts (arguably the more practically impactful scenario) is left as future work, which limits the near-term applicability of the method.

The TTT mechanism optimizes a single scalar (or per-layer scalars) per fixed budget Γ, meaning a new calibration pass is required for every desired compute budget; the paper does not discuss how costly it is to sweep budgets in deployment or whether a single calibrated γ generalizes across budgets (Figure 11 suggests γ is budget-specific), which could limit practicality for applications needing fine-grained runtime control.

strengths: The core idea—decoupling expert selection from expert capacity via slimmable/nested FFN widths—addresses a genuine gap in standard MoE (once an expert is chosen, it always runs at full capacity), and is a natural, well-motivated extension of slimmable-network ideas to the MoE setting.
The training recipe is simple (two forward passes per step, standard MoE auxiliary losses) and requires no changes to the core MoE pipeline, which supports ease of adoption.

The empirical study is broad: multiple model scales (55M to 2.5B from scratch, plus CPT on a 16B DeepSeek-V2-Lite checkpoint), multiple routing regimes (E8A2/E8A4/E16A4/E64A8/E128A8), multiple token budgets, and several inference-time width-assignment strategies (uniform, normalized-probability, shared/layer-wise test-time-trained γ).

The proposed test-time training (TTT) mechanism for width identification is lightweight (a single scalar or one scalar per layer, calibrated on ~50 small batches) yet yields consistent, non-trivial improvements to the compute-quality Pareto frontier across settings, and the learned γ is shown to transfer across datasets (LAMBADA) reasonably well.

Thorough supplementary diagnostics are provided: routing-stability statistics (load CV, entropy, aux loss) comparing full-width vs sampled-width branches, expert-utilization heatmaps, JS-divergence of routing distributions across widths, FLOPs breakdown by component, and an empirical FLOPs-vs-latency/throughput correlation check, which collectively support the internal consistency of the method and partially justify the use of FLOPs as the primary reported metric.
Reproducibility details (architectures, optimizer settings, routing hyperparameters, per-experiment token budgets) are reported in an appendix, aiding replication.
weaknesses: No variance/error bars or multiple seeds are reported for any experiment; given that many reported perplexity/FLOPs improvements are modest (e.g., single-digit percentage point PPL differences), it is hard to assess whether observed gains are statistically meaningful versus noise from a single training run.

The paper does not empirically compare against relevant baselines discussed in Related Work (RoE, Elastic MoE) or against simpler efficiency techniques (e.g., structured pruning, distillation, early-exit, or dynamic depth) despite these being natural comparators for compute-quality trade-off claims; the significance of the contribution relative to existing elastic-inference methods is therefore not empirically substantiated.

Scale remains modest: from-scratch experiments stop at 2.5B parameters/50B tokens, well below current frontier MoE model sizes, and the only larger-scale evidence (DeepSeek-V2-Lite, 16B) is CPT-only rather than full pretraining; the authors acknowledge this as a limitation, but it constrains claims about applicability to state-of-the-art LLMs.

MoSE with uniform width (w=1.0) already outperforms the MoE baseline in several settings (Table 1), suggesting part of the benefit may come from the multi-width training acting as an implicit regularizer rather than from the inference-time width-adaptation mechanism itself; the paper does not disentangle these two effects (e.g., via an ablation training MoSE with only full-width sampling or controlling total training compute equally between MoE and MoSE).

Runtime/latency validation (Appendix B.4) is only conducted for small model/expert configurations (E8A2, E64A8) and does not extend to the larger backbones or the DeepSeek CPT setting where the main efficiency claims are made, leaving open whether FLOPs savings translate to real wall-clock gains at the scales emphasized in the main results (GPT2-Large, DeepSeek-V2-Lite).

Downstream zero-shot reasoning evaluation (Table 2) is reported for only a single model configuration (GPT2-Medium, E8A2), limiting confidence that accuracy gains under width reduction generalize across scales and routing regimes as robustly as the perplexity results.

The router-probability-to-width mapping (power-law scoring with sharpness γ) is heuristic without theoretical grounding; while it empirically works, the design choice (and the choice of budget Γ, discretization step 0.05) is not deeply justified or compared against alternative parameterizations beyond the ablation of fixed vs. learned γ.

strengths: The core idea of decoupling expert selection (routing) from expert capacity (width) is a natural and underexplored extension of MoE conditional computation, combining insights from slimmable/nested networks with sparse MoE routing.

The training recipe (two-width sampling per step) is simple to implement and the paper shows via training-dynamics plots (Fig. 3, Fig. 15) that it does not destabilize optimization relative to standard MoE.

Broad sweep of model scales (55M to 2.5B parameters) and routing configurations (E8A2, E8A4, E16A4, E64A8, E128A8), plus a continual pre-training experiment on a real pretrained MoE checkpoint (DeepSeek-V2-Lite 16B), giving some evidence of generality.

Useful diagnostic appendices (routing-stability CV/entropy/aux-loss comparisons, expert-utilization heatmaps, JS-divergence between width branches, FLOPs breakdown, and latency/throughput correlation) that attempt to rule out confounds such as routing collapse or FLOPs-latency mismatch.

The test-time training (TTT) mechanism for the sharpness parameter γ is lightweight (single/few scalars, 50 calibration batches) and the ablation (Fig. 8) isolates its benefit over a fixed-γ normalized-probability baseline, showing that learning the probability-to-width mapping matters.
weaknesses: Scale is limited: nearly all controlled experiments use GPT2-scale models (55M-2.5B) trained on modest token budgets (3B-50B tokens), far below the scale at which MoE and slimmability interactions are typically evaluated in current literature; the only larger-scale evidence is a single CPT adaptation on DeepSeek-V2-Lite (16B) with no from-scratch validation at that scale, which the paper itself flags as a limitation but does not mitigate.

No direct empirical comparison against the closely related 'Elastic MoE' methods discussed in Related Work (RoE, EMoE) or against Matryoshka/MatFormer-style nested training, despite these being the most relevant baselines for the claimed contribution; the discussion is purely qualitative, leaving open whether MoSE's gains are competitive with or superior to prior elastic-MoE approaches.

Table 1 and most figures report 'lower FLOPs at comparable or better performance' without clearly specifying the exact FLOPs/perplexity matching criterion or tolerance used to compute reported percentage reductions (e.g., 20.3%, 32.8%, 38.1%), making the headline efficiency numbers hard to independently verify or reproduce.

Evaluation is restricted to perplexity and a narrow set of zero-shot benchmarks (LAMBADA, WSC, HellaSwag, PIQA, SIQA); there is no evaluation on knowledge/reasoning-heavy benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K, code) that would better demonstrate relevance for 'efficient and adaptive language models' claims, and no measure of statistical variance/significance is reported across the many plotted curves (apparently single seeds).

The architectural scope is narrow (GPT-2-style decoder-only models plus one DeepSeek-V2-Lite CPT run); no validation on other modern MoE architectures (e.g., shared+routed expert designs, different top-k/capacity regimes used in frontier models) limits confidence that findings transfer beyond the tested setups.

The per-step training overhead of the two-width objective (full width + sampled width) is only qualitatively described as 'lower than two full-width passes' without quantified wall-clock or FLOPs overhead numbers, making it hard to assess the true training-time cost of enabling slimmability versus the inference-time savings obtained.

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap in MoE architectures: once an expert is selected, it is always executed at full capacity, leaving no fine-grained conditional-compute axis within an activated expert. The proposed nested/slimmable expert width mechanism is a natural and simple extension.

Extensive empirical coverage: multiple GPT2 scales (55M–2.5B), several routing regimes (E8A2/E8A4/E16A4/E64A8/E128A8), continual pre-training adaptation on a real pretrained MoE model (DeepSeek-V2-Lite 16B), and zero-shot downstream tasks (HellaSwag, PIQA, SIQA, LAMBADA, WSC).

The test-time training (TTT) mechanism for learning the router-confidence-to-width mapping is lightweight (single or per-layer scalar, 50 calibration batches) and is shown empirically to dominate both uniform-width and fixed-normalized-probability baselines across essentially all settings, which is a clean and convincing ablation (Figure 8).

Good supplementary diagnostics: routing-stability analysis (CV of expert loads, entropy, aux loss, JS-divergence of expert-selection histograms across widths) that directly addresses a natural concern about whether multi-width training destabilizes routing; FLOPs-vs-latency/throughput correlation analysis justifying the FLOPs metric.
Reasonably strong reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, architecture specs, and training schedules are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Scale is modest relative to modern MoE LLMs: from-scratch experiments only go up to 2.5B parameters and 50B tokens; the paper's own limitations section admits it lacks full from-scratch training at frontier MoE scale, so it remains unclear whether gains persist at billion-token-per-parameter / multi-hundred-billion-token training regimes typical of production MoE models.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere in the paper (Table 1, Figures 3-22 all appear to be single runs). Several reported improvements are numerically small (e.g., GPT2-Small 15B OpenWebText PPL: MoE 31.03 vs. MoSE w=1.0 31.26, i.e. MoSE is *worse* at matched full width in that row), making it hard to assess whether observed differences are meaningful versus training noise, especially given WSC has only 273 validation examples.

The TTT calibration set is drawn from the same distribution as several evaluation sets (OpenWebText is used both for pretraining validation and TTT calibration), which raises a methodological concern about whether the reported gains partly reflect calibration-set/eval-set proximity rather than a generalizable width-allocation policy; the LAMBADA transfer experiment (Figure 9) partially mitigates this but is limited to one dataset shift.

No comparison against other conditional-compute / adaptive-inference baselines beyond vanilla MoE (e.g., early-exit transformers, mixture-of-depths, structured pruning of experts, or the discussed Elastic MoE / RoE methods, which are only discussed qualitatively in Related Work but never empirically benchmarked against MoSE despite being closely related contemporaneous methods).

FLOPs-latency correlation (Appendix B.4) is only demonstrated for small models (E8A2/E64A8, presumably GPT2-Small-scale) on specific GPU hardware; it is unclear whether the theoretical FLOPs savings translate to real wall-clock/throughput gains at the larger scales (GPT2-Large, DeepSeek-V2-Lite) where the headline efficiency numbers (32.8%, 38.1% FLOPs reduction) are reported.

The paper reports both accuracy and perplexity for LAMBADA and notes that accuracy is noisy/non-monotonic (Section 3.3), which somewhat undercuts confidence in the zero-shot accuracy gains claimed elsewhere in Table 1 and Table 2, where only accuracy (not perplexity) is reported for the reasoning benchmarks.
